stem: A 15-year-old girl comes to the office with her mother due to amenorrhea.  Menarche occurred at age 12, but she has had no menses for the past several months.  Her mother also says that the patient seems to have stopped growing and that her 14-year-old younger sister has grown taller than her.  The patient's academic activities are unchanged, and she participates in school gymnastics.  She has no history of chronic medical conditions.  Blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg and pulse is 75/min.  BMI is 16.6 kg/m2.  Physical examination shows fine hair on her face and arms.  The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities.  Urine pregnancy test is negative.  Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's amenorrhea?​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​
explanation:
This adolescent has secondary amenorrhea (ie, cessation of menses after menarche).  This patient's low body weight, plateau in height/growth velocity, and lanugo (ie, fine, soft body hair seen with chronic undernutrition) is further suggestive of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.  This condition is commonly seen in those with very low body weight (ie, anorexia nervosa) or in competitive athletes who have relative caloric deficiency due to frequent strenuous exercise (eg, gymnasts).

The underlying pathophysiology of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is incompletely understood but appears to involve reduced circulating leptin levels due to diminished adipose tissue stores.  The decrease in leptin levels inhibits pulsatile GnRH release from the hypothalamus.  Low GnRH suppresses pituitary LH and FSH secretion, causing low circulating estrogen levels, amenorrhea, and reduced peak bone mass.

(Choice B)  Decreased sex hormone-binding globulin production is often present in patients with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS).  This contributes to higher levels of free testosterone, causing irregular menses.  However, PMOS is more commonly diagnosed in overweight women (unlike this patient with low BMI), and patients usually have coarse, terminal hair in androgen-dependent areas (eg, upper lip, chest, back) known as hirsutism (unlike this patient's lanugo hair).

(Choice C)  Testosterone is converted to estrogen in the ovaries (eg, estradiol) and peripheral adipose tissue (eg, estrone) via the enzyme aromatase; however, estrogen is not converted to testosterone in the body.

(Choice D)  Hyperprolactinemia can cause secondary amenorrhea by suppressing normal GnRH release from the hypothalamus and gonadotropin release from the pituitary.  Affected women may also develop galactorrhea.  However, this patient's low BMI and relative caloric deficiency are more consistent with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.

(Choice E)  Neoplastic androgenic hormone production can occur with adrenal and ovarian tumors (eg, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor).  Affected patients have elevated serum androgen levels (eg, dehydroepiandrosterone, testosterone), which can cause secondary amenorrhea.  However, signs of virilization (eg, voice deepening, clitoromegaly) are usually present.

Educational objective:Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea results from loss of pulsatile GnRH release from the hypothalamus.  Loss of cyclic gonadotropin release leads to a decrease in LH and FSH secretion from the pituitary, which in turn causes low circulating estrogen levels.​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​
